sketches.title: The Alibi Cracks
sketches.premise: You and your rival share one alibi, but every turn adds one plain detail to it. Make the story more useful, funny, or dangerously specific without breaking what is already true. The host hypes each new crack and roasts the player when the story folds.
sketches.criterion: The judge accepts one new event that is caused by and fits the whole alibi; a skipped link is a sudden new fact with no setup, an ending is proof, arrest, confession, or everyone leaving the case, and an undo is denying or replacing a detail already standing.
sketches.move_shape: Write one sentence starting with “Then,” naming one event that follows and leaves a fresh problem; example: “Then the cop asks why our muddy shoes match the trail behind the bakery.”
sketches.first_card: Then we both say we were at the all-night diner when the power went out.

sketches.title: Cover Story Kitchen
sketches.premise: Two suspects must cook up one shared alibi, one ingredient at a time. Each move adds a detail that makes the excuse tastier but harder to serve, while the host dishes out savage commentary and calls weak lies burnt garbage.
sketches.criterion: The judge accepts exactly one new alibi detail that follows from every standing detail; a skipped link is a leap from a small clue to a finished explanation, an ending is the alibi being accepted or the mystery solved, and an undo is removing, changing, or contradicting an ingredient already used.
sketches.move_shape: Add one sentence beginning “Then,” with one new detail and a problem it creates; example: “Then the waiter says our table was empty when the alarm rang.”
sketches.first_card: Then we claim we spent the whole night sharing fries in a diner booth.

sketches.title: Witness Switch
sketches.premise: You share an alibi, but every new detail creates someone who might remember it differently. Build a chain of witnesses, places, and awkward proof; the host cheers clever trouble and insults any move that sounds like bargain-bin lying.
sketches.criterion: The judge accepts one next event that grows from the existing alibi and keeps all earlier facts true; a skipped link is introducing a witness or proof without the meeting that creates it, an ending is a witness settling the case, and an undo is making an earlier witness forget or reverse their statement.
sketches.move_shape: Start with “Then,” and add one event that puts the alibi in front of a new witness or piece of proof; example: “Then the cook recognizes my jacket from the security video.”
sketches.first_card: Then we tell the detective we were both waiting for a bus that never came.

sketches.title: Receipt for Trouble
sketches.premise: Your shared alibi must grow through one physical clue at a time: receipts, texts, stains, tickets, and other junk people leave behind. Make each clue support the lie while also creating a nastier question, and let the host scream praise or deliver a brutal roast.
sketches.criterion: The judge accepts one new clue caused by the standing scene and consistent with all its facts; a skipped link is producing a clue that could not have been made or found yet, an ending is a clue that proves the alibi or closes the case, and an undo is destroying, deleting, or changing a clue already shown.
sketches.move_shape: Write “Then,” followed by one event that creates or exposes one new clue and one new opening for trouble; example: “Then my phone prints a receipt for two coffees at 2:13 a.m.”
sketches.first_card: Then we say we spent the night at a closed cinema, nowhere near the crime.

sketches.title: Two Liars, One Night
sketches.premise: Two suspects share a timeline, but the night keeps forcing them to explain where they were and why. Add one connected moment per turn, making the alibi wilder without snapping it; the host narrates like a sports announcer with a mean streak.
sketches.criterion: The judge accepts one event that happens next because of the current timeline and preserves every earlier time and place; a skipped link is jumping across time or distance without travel or cause, an ending is sunrise, rescue, arrest, or a complete explanation, and an undo is sending either suspect back to erase or cancel an earlier event.
sketches.move_shape: Use “Then,” and add one next moment with a clear time, place, or cause; example: “Then, at 11:20, the bakery alarm forces us to hide in its delivery van.”
sketches.first_card: Then, at 10:00 p.m., we tell the police we were together on the last train home.

sketches.title: Alibi Under Crossfire
sketches.premise: One shared alibi faces a fresh question every turn, and the answer must create the next question instead of ending the case. Keep the lie alive through connected events while the host fires off hype, filthy suspicion, and roast-level jabs.
sketches.criterion: The judge accepts one event that answers or complicates the latest question while fitting the entire transcript; a skipped link is answering a question with an unsupported final fact, an ending is a flawless answer, confession, or the questioner giving up, and an undo is taking back an answer or making an old fact false.
sketches.move_shape: Begin with “Then,” answer the current question through one visible event, and leave a new question behind; example: “Then the bartender shows the tab, but it has my name and a stranger’s card.”
sketches.first_card: Then the detective asks why both our phones stopped moving at midnight.
